source.title: The Open Materials 2024 (OMat24) inorganic materials dataset and models
source.authors: Luis Barros-Luque; Muhammed Shuaibi; Xiang Fu; Brandon M. Wood; Misko Dzamba; Meng Gao; Ammar Rizvi; Matthew Uyttendaele; C. Zitnick; Zachary W. Ulissi

record.tranche_reason: Reports a training-data-size learning curve for materials interatomic potentials, a different modality from language modeling. It does not test language-model scaling laws directly.
record.gate_note: The study does not evaluate held-out language-model cross-entropy, parameter-count or compute scaling, compute-optimal allocation, or architecture variation at fixed parameter count. Its own relevant result is a materials-model prediction-error learning curve versus training-set size; numerical curve values are not stated in the text. Results cited from other studies are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: This is mainly a dataset and model paper for machine-learning interatomic potentials. Its own Supplementary Figure D.1 gives energy and force MAE learning curves against training-set size (about 1e5 to 1e8 structures) for eSEN. That is a data-scaling result in a non-text modality, so it bears on V5. The test is weak: there is no power-law fit, no exponent, and no numbers in the text. Table H.1 also gives test errors for three EquiformerV2 sizes, but the rows do not record them.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase covers only a supplementary learning-curve remark. The authors' main conclusions are different. OMat24, with over 110M diverse non-equilibrium DFT calculations, lets models reach state-of-the-art Matbench-Discovery results (F1 0.925, energy-above-hull MAE 18 meV/atom). It also greatly reduces or removes systematic softening across architectures. In the supplement they note that eSEN error falls with dataset size and plateaus at about 100M samples.
record.recipe_differences: Materials interatomic-potential prediction-error learning curves versus dataset size; not language-model pretraining cross-entropy scaling.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported learning curve is for the eSEN architecture; the text says the error plateaus at approximately 100 million samples.
record.problems: The relevant learning curve is for one named architecture, exact curve values are not stated in the text, and no power-law fit or exponent is reported; the study concerns materials models rather than language models.

untested.parts: Power-law form, exponents and range in materials models; image, video, repeated-data and fine-tuning regimes. The one parameter-size comparison (eqV2-S/M/L) has only three points, and those models also change depth and Lmax.
Not tested: no language-model loss scaling.
Not tested: no relation between scale or loss and downstream benchmark results is analysed.

missing.what: Test MAE for eqV2-S (31M), eqV2-M (87M) and eqV2-L (154M) trained on OMat24. Errors fall with size, e.g. WBM energy 15.96 → 14.87 → 14.57 meV/atom. The sizes also differ in depth and Lmax. The eSEN-30M row duplicates the eqV2-S values, which looks like a table error.
missing.locator: Supplementary Table H.1; Table G.1; Table G.4

missing.what: Matbench-Discovery results across eqV2 sizes after fine-tuning, e.g. MAE 24 (S), 20 (M), 19 (L) meV/atom with MPtrj-sAlex fine-tuning. These are downstream gains with parameter count over three points.

record.verdict_notes: The only scaling-related evidence is in the supplement and is qualitative in the text. Figure D.1 is log-log, but its values cannot be read from the extracted text. No verdict is given: the rows cannot show power-law form, and the reported plateau may be a fixed-capacity effect. That reading rests on the authors' own wording, 'provided the model has sufficient capacity'. The paper cites Kaplan et al. only to motivate large datasets.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss versus parameter count, tokens, and compute.
Extrapolation of language-model scaling fits from small runs to much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.

The study reports materials-model prediction errors versus training-set size, but does not fit or establish a power-law form. It does not test image/video models, repeated data, or fine-tuning and transfer as scaling regimes.
Downstream task performance as a function of pretraining loss or scale.
Dependence of scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits on fitting choices, and systematic departures from power laws.

rows.subject: eSEN
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated energy prediction error on OMat24 training subsamples of increasing size.
rows.value: Prediction errors decrease as dataset size increases; the error plateaus at approximately 100 million samples.
rows.note: The prose reports the decrease and approximate plateau; exact values and a power-law fit are not stated.
rows.check: The text says only that errors decrease and then plateau at about 100M samples. With no values or fit, the power-law form V5 names cannot be checked. The plateau comes from a single fixed-size model (eSEN, about 30M parameters), and the authors make the decrease conditional on the model having 'sufficient capacity'. It may therefore be a capacity bottleneck, which the version's 'others not the bottleneck' condition excludes. That makes 'partial' an over-reading.

rows.subject: eSEN
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated force prediction error on OMat24 training subsamples of increasing size.
rows.value: Prediction errors decrease as dataset size increases; the error plateaus at approximately 100 million samples.
rows.note: The prose reports the decrease and approximate plateau; exact values and a power-law fit are not stated.
rows.check: Same as D1-energy: prose only, no fit or values, and the plateau may reflect fixed model capacity rather than a departure from the law.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
